nameStory: The 'eight-spotted' part of this tiny bee's name comes from the distinctive pattern of light-colored spots adorning its dark body - though you'll need sharp eyes or a magnifying glass to count them! It's called a 'fairy bee' because members of the Perdita genus are among the smallest bees in North America, so delicate and diminutive they seem almost magical when you spot one hovering around flowers.
description: The Eight-spotted Fairy Bee is a tiny, solitary bee that's one of the smallest you'll encounter in New England. These delicate insects have dark bodies decorated with pale yellow or whitish spots, giving them their distinctive name. Like other fairy bees, they're much smaller than honeybees or bumblebees, and they nest in the ground rather than in hives. Despite their tiny size, they're important native pollinators that visit a variety of wildflowers.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - noticeably tinier than any other bee you're likely to see, appearing almost gnat-like in flight until you notice the bee-like behavior

idTips.label: Spots
idTips.description: Eight pale yellowish or whitish spots scattered across the dark body, though you may need a close look or magnifying glass to count them clearly

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Overall dark brown to black body with a subtle metallic sheen when caught in good light

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting flight low to the ground and around flowers, more erratic than larger bees

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen visiting small wildflowers, frequently landing on petals rather than burrowing deep into blooms like larger bees

habitat: Look for Eight-spotted Fairy Bees in open, sunny areas with sandy or well-drained soils where they can excavate their tiny ground nests. They're often found in meadows, old fields, and woodland edges with abundant small wildflowers. These bees prefer areas with sparse vegetation where the soil is exposed, making nesting sites accessible.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from underground nests as temperatures warm, with peak activity typically starting in late spring when wildflowers become abundant.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for adults, when you'll see them visiting flowers and females excavating small nests in sandy soil. Look for tiny holes in bare ground.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down as adults complete their life cycle, though some late-emerging individuals may still be active in early fall.
seasonality.winter: Overwinter as larvae or pupae in underground nests, completely inactive and not observable above ground.

funFact: These tiny bees are so small that a single teaspoon could hold dozens of them, yet each female is capable of excavating her own underground nest tunnel that can be several inches deep - imagine digging a tunnel 50 times your own height with just your hands and teeth!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be mistaken for tiny flies or gnats until you observe their bee-like flower-visiting behavior and slightly fuzzy bodies. Unlike flies, they have the characteristic narrow 'wasp waist' of bees and move more deliberately from flower to flower.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'miner bee' (from their family Andrenidae) refers to their ground-nesting habits, but don't confuse this with damage to your garden - these tiny bees are beneficial pollinators whose small nests cause no harm to lawns or landscaping.
compareHints: Among New England's fairy bees, the Eight-spotted Fairy Bee is distinguished by its specific pattern of eight pale spots, while relatives like the Ground-cherry Fairy Bee may have different spot arrangements or be associated with different host plants. The Sandbar Willow Fairy Bee is typically found near wetland willows rather than in the drier habitats preferred by the eight-spotted species.
